From the ground · what the right instruments see

Geophones: what instruments on the ground see

Before judging a satellite, ask what the instruments built for the job can see. Geophysicists image the shallow ground with arrays of geophones and a source, hammer blows or the ambient hum, and invert the records into a three-dimensional tomogram. Here that is done in simulation, over the same ground the satellite was flown over. Boreholes, echo imaging and full-waveform inversion find the chamber; the lab’s tools find it when the physics allows, so the satellite’s failure is the satellite’s.

Every tomogram here is scored against a truth the method never saw

The ground is composed first, from sourced materials. The waves are computed through it by a solver that knows nothing about any inversion. The inversions see only what the sensors recorded, with noise, on a different grid. Whatever they draw is then compared with the chambers that are really there.

compose

Known ground

Test benches from one chamber to the claimed underworld, and Giza. Strata, sand cover, water table and von Kármán heterogeneity, all as data. See them in the underworld.

simulate

Waves through it

3-D isotropic elastic velocity–stress finite differences, fourth order in space, absorbing boundaries on the sides and floor, a free surface on top, air-filled chambers as traction-free cavities.

recover

What practitioners would draw

Travel-time tomography, ambient-noise tomography and full-waveform inversion, each run as it would be run in the field, then scored voxel by voxel.

The solver matches exact solutions to within a fraction of a percent

Before it touches a chamber, the forward model is checked where the answer is known exactly, in Mokattam limestone (P 3,300 m/s, S 1,830 m/s).

Travel times catch the chamber's shadow from boreholes, and nothing from the surface

The one-chamber bench: a 6 m air-filled cube, its top 12 m down, in bare limestone. Every record comes from the solver above, with noise 30 dB below each record's peak; first arrivalsfirst break seismicThe first arrival of energy on a seismic record. Its timing, picked on every record, is the data of travel-time tomography. are picked by waveform correlation; the picks are inverted on a 1 m grid by a code that never sees the model. Air is 90% slower than the rock; a first arrival goes around the void instead of through it, so what travel times can see is the delay of the detour.

-11.3%speed recovered inside the chamber from four boreholescrosshole · 36 shots, 104 sensors
3.5×the chamber's anomaly against the tomogram's own scatter around itcrosshole
+0.0%speed recovered inside the chamber from the surfacesurface · 25 shots, 81 geophones
0.44ms95th-percentile pick error against straight rays, the precision the picks carrycrosshole picks

Crosshole rays through the chamber recover it as a slow patch of -11% (air would be -90%): first arrivals bend around a void, so travel-time tomography sees its shadow, not its emptiness. From the surface, with the direct P picked on 16 stacked blows, the same method recovers +0.0%: in uniform rock no first-arrival ray reaches 12 m.

The chamber's echo, too faint to see on any record, images it from the surface

The same hammer and geophone grids that saw nothing by travel times. Records are made twice, with and without the chamber; the difference is its echo. On a typical record that echo is 21 dB below the waves and 6 dB below the noise. Sent back through the rock by reverse-time migrationreverse-time migration seismicImaging by sending recorded waves backwards through a model of the ground and marking where they meet the waves sent forward from the source. It is the first step of full-waveform inversion., 25 shots and 81 geophones add up where the echo came from. The rock without the chamber is known exactly here, so this is the most favourable case for any waveform method: the first step of full-waveform inversionfull-waveform inversion seismicFitting whole seismic records, not just arrival times, by adjusting a model of the ground; each step is a gradient computed by propagating the misfit backwards in time., taken with a perfect starting model.

Noise stands in for the hammer, but its image of the chamber tops out at 2.2×, however long it listens

No hammer: 48 noise sources scattered over the ground around the same geophone grid, each a stream of random vertical pushes, like footsteps and traffic. Cross-correlating the noise at two geophones gives the wave one would send the other (interferometryambient-noise interferometry seismicCross-correlating the background hum recorded at two sensors turns it into the wave that would travel from one to the other, so noise can stand in for a source.), so every geophone becomes a virtual sourcevirtual source seismicA sensor made to act as a source: the correlation of its noise record with another sensor’s is the wave a real source there would have sent. Noise sources spread over the ground give it as minus the lag derivative of the correlation.. 16 of them are used as in echo imaging: the gathers predicted without the chamber are subtracted and what remains is migrated. The rock is known exactly and the noise field is averaged over an unlimited record, the most favourable passive case; a finite record adds fluctuations whose image falls as one over the square root of its length.

0.90correlation of the wave retrieved from noise with a real source's, 16 m apartminus the lag derivative of the noise correlation
2.2×the passive image at the chamber against the image elsewhere, with an unlimited recordactive echo imaging: 6.0×
neverof noise for the chamber to stand at 3× the rest of the imagefluctuations scaled from a 10 s realisation
7.3mfrom the chamber's centre to the brightest point of the passive imageimage below 3 m

Noise correlations reproduce the wave between two geophones (correlation 0.90 with a real source). With the rock known exactly and an unlimited record, the passive echo image is 2.2x brighter around the chamber than elsewhere, and its brightest point lies 7 m from the chamber's centre. No record length reaches 3x: even averaged forever, the chamber's part of the correlations images away from it at 46% of its brightness around it.

Fitting whole records from a practitioner’s start finds the chamber as a −15.8% drop in S speed, 5.7× the scatter

The same noisy surface records echo imaging migrated, now fitted whole by full-waveform inversionfull-waveform inversion seismicFitting whole seismic records, not just arrival times, by adjusting a model of the ground; each step is a gradient computed by propagating the misfit backwards in time.. Unlike echo imaging, the rock is not given: the start is what a practitioner would have, uniform rock at the P speed the surface travel times gave (3,259 m/s) and an S speed from the textbook ratio √3 (1,881 m/s, 3% fast). Gradients of P and S speed come from correlating forward and adjoint stresses, checked against finite differences; traces within 4 m of their hammer are left out, and the iterations stop at the noise level or after ten; here after ten, just above it. The records were made with the same solver and grid the inversion uses (the “inverse crime”): the most favourable case for FWI, softened only by the noise and the wrong start.

-15.8%S speed recovered inside the chamber5.7× the scatter around it
-2.4%P speed recovered inside the chamber2.2× the scatter
1,866m/sbackground S speed after inversion, from 1,881true 1,830 m/s
0.37misfit left after 10 iterations, where the noise alone leaves 0.332,000 of 2,025 traces

From uniform rock at the travel-time P speed and a textbook S speed, ten iterations fitting the whole records bring the misfit to 0.37 of its start, against 0.33 for the noise alone. The chamber comes back as -15.8% in S speed, 5.7× the scatter around it, its slowest cell 1.8 m from the chamber's centre, in its upper half; in P speed only -2.4%. The background S speed moves from 1,881 to 1,866 m/s, toward the true 1,830. Of the surface methods, this is the only one to put the chamber where it is with the rock not given, in the most favourable case.

The arrays are the ones near-surface surveys actually deploy

Active

A grid of three-component geophones at 1 to 4 m spacing and a source walked across it (hammer or weight drop), with realistic source repeatability and sensor self-noise.

Passive

A dense nodal array recording the ambient hum of traffic, wind and visitors. It is the seismic cousin of the radar claim: natural vibration asked to reveal what lies below.

Three inversions, from the classic to the state of the art

Travel-time tomographytravel-time tomography seismicFinding the speed of the ground from how long first arrivals take between many sources and receivers, by tracing their rays and adjusting the speeds until the times fit.

First arrivals picked from the records, bent rays traced through an eikonal solver, a regularised least-squares update. Robust, and blurred at a wavelength.

Ambient-noise tomographyambient-noise interferometry seismicCross-correlating the background hum recorded at two sensors turns it into the wave that would travel from one to the other, so noise can stand in for a source.

Noise cross-correlated between sensor pairs becomes the wave that would travel between them. In practice its surface-wave dispersion is inverted for shear speed with depth; here the correlations serve as virtual sourcesvirtual source seismicA sensor made to act as a source: the correlation of its noise record with another sensor’s is the wave a real source there would have sent. Noise sources spread over the ground give it as minus the lag derivative of the correlation. for echo imaging, the most a passive array can do.

Full-waveform inversionfull-waveform inversion seismicFitting whole seismic records, not just arrival times, by adjusting a model of the ground; each step is a gradient computed by propagating the misfit backwards in time.

The whole record fitted by adjoint-state gradients, from low frequencies up. The sharpest images near-surface geophysics makes, and the most demanding.

Detectability is a map over size, depth and array, not a yes or no

For each method and each chamber: the contrast recovered at the chamber against the spread of the background, the error in position and size, and the false chambers drawn elsewhere. Swept over chamber size, depth, array aperture, spacing and frequency, the result would be a map of where seismology succeeds and where it stops. The satellite, judged on the same ground, is beyond that map’s edge (the satellite).
